topic: The Neural Library: How MLPs in Transformers Store Facts
target_audience: University students in computer science or AI-enthusiasts with basic linear algebra knowledge

sections.title: The Mystery of the Knowledge Base
sections.content: Introduce the paradox: Transformers are known for processing sequences (Attention), but where is the 'encyclopedia' stored? Identify the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) blocks, which contain roughly 2/3 of a model's parameters, as the likely storage for factual knowledge.
sections.example: Imagine a robot named 'Lexi' who knows that 'Eiffel Tower' is in 'Paris'. While the Attention mechanism looks at the words around her, the MLP acts as her internal library card catalog.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Key-Value Memory Systems
sections.content: Explain the abstract concept of associative memory. A 'Key' is a pattern to look for, and a 'Value' is the information associated with it. Visualize this as a dictionary where looking up a word (Key) gives you a definition (Value).
sections.example: Think of a vending machine: The code 'A1' is the Key; the actual bag of chips released is the Value.

sections.title: Anatomy of an MLP: The Two-Step Mechanism
sections.content: Break down the MLP into two linear transformations with a non-linear activation (ReLU/GELU). Visually represent the first matrix (W1) as a set of 'Key' detectors and the second matrix (W2) as a set of 'Value' injectors. Mathematically, show y = f(x · W1) · W2.
sections.example: Visual: Matrix W1 is a wall of 'lock holes' (keys). Matrix W2 is a tray of 'prizes' (values). If the input vector 'fits' a lock in W1, the corresponding prize in W2 is pushed into the model's workflow.

sections.title: The Activation Trigger (The ReLU Gate)
sections.content: Explain the role of the non-linear activation function. If the input vector matches a 'Key' in W1, the neuron 'fires' (activates). If it doesn't match, the output is zero. This ensures only relevant facts are retrieved for the current context.
sections.example: Graphical: A line graph showing a 'threshold'. If the 'Eiffel Tower' signal is strong enough, the gate opens; if we are talking about 'Eiffel's blueprint', a different key might trigger.

sections.title: Information Injection into the Residual Stream
sections.content: Describe the 'Residual Stream' as a moving conveyor belt of information. The MLP doesn't replace the data; it adds a 'Knowledge Vector' to the stream. Show the vector addition: x_new = x_old + MLP(x_old).
sections.example: Visual: A boat (the word 'Paris') floating down a river. As it passes the MLP station, a crane drops a 'Capital of France' package onto the boat, making the information more complete.

sections.title: The Superposition: Storing Billions of Facts
sections.content: Address how so many facts fit. In high-dimensional space, vectors can be 'nearly orthogonal' (almost 90 degrees apart). This allows thousands of 'Keys' to exist in the same MLP layer without interfering with each other.
sections.example: Visual: A 3D sphere where thousands of pins (fact vectors) are stuck. Even though the sphere is small, the pins don't touch because there is so much 'space' in higher dimensions.

sections.title: Summary & Conclusion
sections.content: Recap the 5-minute journey: MLPs are not just math functions; they are associative memories. W1 recognizes the context (Key), and W2 provides the fact (Value). Together, they turn a sequence processor into a knowledgeable assistant.
sections.example: Lexi the Robot successfully answers 'Paris' because her MLP 'Key' for 'Capital of France' fired and injected the correct 'Value' into her thought stream.
